# Defining a Minimal Benchmark for Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Calculators in New England EHR-derived Cohort

**Authors:** Zinzuwadia Aniket; Mineeva Olga; Li Chunying; Farukhi Zareen; Giulianini Franco; Cade Brian; Chen Lin; Karlson Elizabeth; Paynter Nina; Mora Samia; Demler Olga

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School | 2ETH Zurich | 3Brigham & Women’s Hospital | 4Massachusetts General Hospital

Extensive research has produced numerous ASCVD risk prediction tools, with over 363 published models between the years 2004 and 2013.1 Proposed models strive to improve upon previous guidelines-recommended models by incorporating additional clinical information (genetic variants, biomarkers, social deprivation status) or leveraging ML models for complex pattern recognition. Interestingly, studies in large observational cohorts have shown that models based solely on age, sex, and race can capture up to 80% of the performance of guideline-recommended tools.2 Hence, the added value of complex models beyond a basic locally-derived one remains uncertain. We propose establishing a benchmark for the minimum acceptable discriminative performance of any cardiovascular risk calculator when assessing its suitability for external populations. We use the c-statistic, ranging from 0.5 for random guessing to 1.0 for perfect prediction, generated by basic benchmark models derived solely from demographic data readily available in health systems. Accordingly, we derive benchmark models from three demographic variables and compare them to the PCE, a guidelines-recommended models in the United States, in a EHR-derived New England cohort.

We utilized retrospective data from the Mass General Brigham Research Patient Data Registry, a EHR repository from Boston-area hospitals. Patients with prior ASCVD events (first occurrence of myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular death) during the observation period (1997–2006) were excluded. The outcome was defined as an incident ASCVD event over a 10-year period (2007–2016). Patients with statin use in the observation period were excluded and patients who initiated statin use in the follow-up period were censored at the date of statin initiation. Events were identified using ML disease phenotypes, ICD codes, and cause of death obtained from the Massachusetts Department of Public Health and National Death Index.3 The study included 64,773 patients (ages 55–79 in 2007) with complete variables for PCE calculation. Race-specific PCE equations were used for Black and White populations; for other racial groups, White PCE equations were applied, as per guidelines. Cox proportional hazards benchmark models were fit in a training set (comprising 50% of the overall data) that included demographic information such as age, race/ethnicity, and sex as predictor variables. Model discrimination for PCE and benchmark models was evaluated using the Uno c-statistic in the test set (remaining 50% of data). The MGB Institutional Review Board waived informed consent and approved the study protocol. Summary data is available upon request from the corresponding author, while person-level data is restricted to affiliated researchers for approved projects.

In the test set of 32,391 patients, the median [IQR] age was 63 [58–69] years with 38% being men. Patients had a self-reported race/ethnicity of White (26,972), Black (1,691), Hispanic (1,087), Asian (777) and other patients (1,864). Additional clinical characteristics are reported in Table 1. The overall ASCVD 10-year event rate was 4.3%, varying by race/ethnicity: 4.4% for White, 4.7% for Black, 2.4% for Hispanic, and 2.9% for Asian patients. The median [IQR] estimated 10-year PCE risk for the overall cohort was 9.7% [4.7%–18.5%]. PCE showed moderate discriminative performance (c-statistic 0.74[95% CI: 0.72–0.76]) in the overall cohort. Compared to PCE, two benchmark models (age/sex/race and age/sex) exhibited similar discriminative performance (0.72[0.70–0.74]). We also observed a similar c-statistic (0.74[0.72–0.76]) when we applied these benchmark models to cardiovascular death which was obtained from death records review from government registries. Age (0.69[0.67–0.70]) and sex (0.60[0.58–0.62]) alone had lower discriminative performance.

To mitigate informed presence bias, we only included patients with high EHR data-completeness score, relied on validated and adjudicated (in a subsample) disease phenotypes, and integrated cause of death information from two government registries.3 To attenuate for varying dates of risk factor measurement, we used measurements closest to 2007 to estimate 10-year risk from 2007–2016. The c-statistic of PCE in this cohort was comparable to that reported in other external validations, indicating similar cardiovascular risk structure.4 Recent risk prognostic tools have replaced race with alternative biomarkers to account for race-based differences in clinical risk.5 However, we ultimately report results of a benchmark model including race because it is readily available with high rates of data-completeness across health records, and it is unclear if its equivalent performance to a race-free model is due to being evaluated in a relatively homogenous cohort (>80% White). Race-free minimal benchmarks should be furthered explored in multi-ethnic cohorts.

Our results indicate that locally derived Cox models with only age, sex and race have c-statistic of 0.72[0.70–0.74] in a set-aside training set. This level is similar to the c-statistics of a well-established ASCVD risk tool, setting a high bar for minimal acceptable performance for cardiovascular risk prediction calculators in this cohort. If external validation of established risk calculators, like PCE, shows similar performance to locally derived models incorporating basic demographic factors, it suggests the need for model refitting or revision. This benchmarking approach offers future research an objective standard for assessing risk models in local populations.

# Congenitally Fused Cervical Spine Is Associated With Adjacent-Level Degeneration in the Absence of Cervical Spine Surgery

**Authors:** Gabriel N Friedman; Benjamin L Grannan; Aniket Zinzuwadia; Ziv M Williams; Jean-Valery Coumans

**Affiliations:** *Department of Neurosurgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA; | ‡Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA; | §Department of Neurosurgery, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA

## Abstract

Cervical fusion surgery is associated with adjacent-level degeneration, but surgical and technical factors are difficult to dissociate from the mechanical effects of the fusion itself.

To determine the effect of fusion on adjacent-level degeneration in unoperated patients using a cohort of patients with congenitally fused cervical vertebrae.

We identified 96 patients with incidental single-level cervical congenital fusion on computed tomography imaging. We compared these patients to an age-matched control cohort of 80 patients without congenital fusion. We quantified adjacent-level degeneration through direct measurements of intervertebral disk parameters as well as the validated Kellgren & Lawrence classification scale for cervical disk degeneration. Ordinal logistic regression and 2-way analysis of variance testing were performed to correlate extent of degeneration with the congenitally fused segment.

Nine hundred fifty-five motion segments were analyzed. The numbers of patients with C2-3, C3-4, C4-5, C5-6, and C6-7 congenitally fused segments were 47, 11, 11, 17, and 9, respectively. We found that patients with congenital fusion at C4-C5 and C5-C6 had a significantly greater extent of degeneration at adjacent levels compared with the degree of degeneration at the same levels in control patients and in patients with congenital fusion at other cervical levels, even while controlling for expected degeneration and age.

Taken together, our data suggest that congenitally fused cervical spinal segments at C4-C5 and C5-C6 are associated with adjacent-level degeneration independent of fixation instrumentation. This study design removes surgical factors that might contribute to adjacent-level degeneration.

KEY WORDS: Adjacent-level degeneration/disease, Congenital fusion, Cervical spine

Adjacent segment degeneration and disease are well-established sequelae of cervical spine fusion, affecting sizable proportions of patients undergoing instrumented fusion procedures.1 Radiographic rates of adjacent-level degeneration have been reported in 39% to 67% of patients who have undergone anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) procedures, while rates of clinical adjacent segment disease are estimated in around 19% of patients.2-5 Ultimately, 8% to 16% of these patients undergo revision surgery secondary to adjacent segment disease.6-9

There is considerable controversy regarding the etiology of adjacent segment degeneration.10 Several postsurgical factors have been implicated: increased motion at the adjacent level,11 altered biomechanical stresses from heightened loading pressures,12 and iatrogenic violation of the anterior longitudinal ligament attachment.13 In addition, industry-sponsored reports have demonstrated higher rates of adjacent segment degeneration after ACDF compared with cervical disk arthroplasty.14,15 Nevertheless, numerous authors have also speculated that adjacent segment degeneration may simply reflect the ongoing progression of a chronic degenerative process that necessitated the index procedure in the first place.16 With evidence on each side of the debate, the precise cause of adjacent segment disease has been labeled a major open question in the field of cervical spine surgery.17,18

Cervical congenital fusion is a rare segmentation anomaly that provides a model for better understanding the effects of vertebral fusion independent of surgical or technical factors. Although previous research has correlated cervical congenital fusion with adjacent degeneration and cervical myelopathy,19,20 these studies have been limited by small patient cohorts and inclusion of patients with Klippel-Feil syndrome, which entails confounding considerations because of the presence of multiple fused vertebrae and other anatomic variations.

Here, we have assembled the largest cohort of patients with cervical congenital fusion in the reported literature (by several multiples) to investigate whether the presence of block vertebrae results in adjacent segment degeneration. Importantly, we excluded patients with a diagnosis of Klippel-Feil syndrome. The finding of increased degeneration at levels specifically adjacent to the congenitally fused motion segment would argue in favor of the hypothesis that adjacent segment degeneration results from the presence of a fused motion segment, as opposed to factors related to surgical technique or an ongoing process of cervical spondylosis.

## METHODS

### Study Data

Patient data were obtained from the Research Patient Data Registry, a centralized clinical data repository for the Mass General Brigham hospital system. This study was approved by the Mass General Brigham Human Research Office/Institutional Review Board. Individual patient consent was not required within this protocol. We performed a free-text search for all patients that provided a match for “congenital fusion” and related search terms within radiology reports for cervical spine computed tomography (CT) imaging. Patients with partial congenital fusion, multiple fused levels, congenital syndromes such as Klippel-Feil, prior cervical spine surgery, and those younger than 10 years were excluded. We identified 96 patients with single-level congenital fusion of the cervical spine. For patients with multiple CT imaging studies, the first study available was used for the main analysis. Given that most of these patients were imaged incidentally in the setting of a fall, we also identified an age-matched cohort of 95 age-matched control patients who were also imaged in the setting of a fall. A total of 15 patients were excluded from this cohort for prior cervical spine surgery (9), fracture (2), unavailable imaging (2), acute disk herniation (1), and partial congenital fusion (1). Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine files were obtained for all relevant studies, and imaging analysis was performed using Osirix software (Pixmeo).

### Clinical Assessments

To evaluate disk and facet joint degeneration, we used the grading criteria originally developed by Kellgren et al21 that has subsequently been adapted and validated for use in the cervical spine (Tables 1 and 2).22,23 This grading system was used because it has previously been recommended for clinical use over other cervical disk degeneration grading systems based on its interobserver reliability statistics.24 To obtain disk degeneration score measurements, each motion segment was evaluated in the sagittal plane and assigned a score from 0 to 4, with 0 representing no radiographic evidence of degeneration and 4 indicating multiple large osteophytes, severe disk space narrowing, and severe sclerosis. Anterior, middle, and posterior disk heights were also measured within the Osirix application. Measurements were performed by a senior neurosurgery resident (G.N.F) and compared with those performed by an attending neurosurgeon (J.V.C.). An inter-rater reliability score of 0.63 was calculated using Krippendorff alpha coefficient, demonstrating a good level of agreement. Because the patient cohort was obtained from the centralized hospital system database, graders were independent of care for the patients included in this study. Patient information, including age at the time of imaging and indication for imaging, was obtained through the electronic medical record.

### Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis was performed with Python version 3.7 through Jupyter notebook and SPSS (IBM). Differences in patient age between fusion and control groups were performed using two-way t test analysis, while difference in age between subgroups was accomplished using 1-way analysis of variance testing. Statistical testing for sex differences between the fusion and control cohort was performed using χ2 testing. Analysis of degenerative disk disease and facet joint degeneration scores was performed using ordinal logistic regression. To dissociate the effect of age on degeneration, ordinal logistical regression with age as a covariate was also performed. Analysis of disk height differences was performed using the independent t test. Direct comparison of the excess degeneration scores (mean degeneration at a fused level minus the expected degeneration based on control measurements) for adjacent vs nonadjacent levels was also performed using the independent t test. The threshold for statistical significance was P < .05. Supervised learning analysis was performed using a one vs rest support vector classifier from the scikit-learn Python toolkit. In this implementation, we defined 4 different classes: levels that were adjacent to a midcervical fused segment, levels adjacent to other fused segments (ie, not midcervical), levels that were nonadjacent in patients with congenital fusion, and levels from control patients (by definition nonadjacent). For a given motion segment, the model was trained on the patient's age, degeneration score of the specific motion segment, level of the specific motion segment (eg, C2-3 and C3-4), and class membership. Half of the data were randomly selected for model training while the other half were used for model testing to generate receiver operating characteristics.

## RESULTS

We identified 96 patients with single-level congenital fusion in the cervical spine. In 76% of patients, this finding was noted in the setting of workup for a fall or trauma. Other indications for imaging were workup of a mass or swelling (11%), pain (9%), and weakness (2%). Among the congenital fusion cohort, the numbers of patients with C2-3, C3-4, C4-5, C5-6, C6-7, and C7-T1 congenitally fused segments were 47, 11, 11, 17, 9, and 1 respectively (see Figure 1 for representative images). The single patient with C7-T1 was excluded from further analysis. Patients with congenital fusion were, on average, age 51.0 years (SD = 20.6 years), while patients in the control cohort were, on average, age 51.7 years (SD = 21.7 years). There was no significant difference in age or sex composition of the 2 groups (Table 3).

In patients with C4-C5 congenital fusion, degeneration scores were higher at adjacent levels C3-C4 (2.73 vs 0.95, P < .0001, ordinal logistic regression) and C5-C6 (3.00 vs 1.85, P = .003, ordinal logistic regression) compared with degeneration at these levels in control patients. Although the populations of the congenital fusion cohort patients at C4-C5 and C5-C6 were slightly older than the control patients (see Supplemental Digital Content 3, Table, http://links.lww.com/NEU/D689), there was no significant difference between the ages of patients across fusion groups (P = .13, 1-way analysis of variance). Furthermore, when we performed ordinal logistic regression with age as a covariate, while we found an expected effect of age on degeneration, our findings related to adjacent-level degeneration were unchanged (see Supplemental Digital Content 4, Table, http://links.lww.com/NEU/D690).

Although patients with congenital fusion at C4-C5 and C5-C6 demonstrated elevated degeneration at adjacent levels, they also demonstrated higher overall levels of degeneration. However, we found that degeneration scores were significantly higher at adjacent levels compared with nonadjacent levels in these patients, when controlling for the expected degree of degeneration at each level (P = .004, 2-way t test, Figure 4). Furthermore, in patients with congenital fusion at C2-C3, C3-C4, and C6-C7, we found that there was no significant difference in degeneration scores at adjacent vs nonadjacent levels, when controlled for expected degree of degeneration by the level (P = .19, 2-way t test, Figure 4).

## DISCUSSION

Nationally, there has been a debate on the utility of fusion vs motion preservation in management of cervical stenosis. Advocates of cervical fusion argue that it results in long-term outcome improvement and that range of motion is not related to adjacent segment degeneration.25,26 Meanwhile, advocates of motion preservation argue that arthroplasty has the potential to reduce adjacent segment disease by minimizing biomechanical stresses, including intradiscal pressures, at adjacent levels.27,28 Our mechanistic understanding of adjacent segment disease remains incomplete. At the most simplistic level, it is possible that adjacent-level degeneration can be fully explained by loss of movement. Some authors have also hypothesized that technical factors at time of surgery play a role.29 These factors include disruption of the anterior longitudinal ligament,5 the placement of an anterior cervical plate or interbody device,30 and even seeding of the surgical field with P. acnes.31

In attempting to characterize the pure mechanistic effects, we selected patients for our study that had congenital fusion with no other syndromic anatomic abnormalities (which have been common in other investigations analyzing patients with congenital fusion19,20). In doing so, we sought to quantify the degree of adjacent-level degeneration that can be attributed solely to the loss of movement by eliminating surgical factors. We used a comprehensive search strategy that allowed us to identify the largest reported cohort of patients with congenital fusion.

We found that not all cervical levels are equally susceptible to degeneration. We found higher rates of adjacent segment degeneration in patients with congenital fusion at C4-C5 and C5-C6, whereas patients with congenital fusion at C2-C3, C3-C4, and C6-C7 did not demonstrate increased levels of degeneration at adjacent levels. This finding may inform surgical strategy, especially when considering the choice of fusion vs motion preservation (eg, an ACDF at C3-4 carries less risk of adjacent segment degeneration compared with an ACDF at C4-C5). Motion preservation techniques (disk arthroplasty or posterior foraminotomy) may be reasonable for younger patients undergoing single-level procedures in the midcervical spine.

Intriguingly, our results, in many ways, mirror reported findings in the literature on adjacent segment disease after ACDF. For instance, similar to our findings, Hilibrand et al32 found that the C5-C6 and C6-7 levels were at greatest risk for adjacent segment disease. The reason that adjacent segment degeneration seems to be most prominent in the midcervical spine has not been fully established; however, one possibility is related to motion restriction in proximity to the cervicothoracic junction.33

There seems to be a wide divergence between adjacent segment degeneration and clinically relevant adjacent segment disease. For example, Yue et al,34 found that 73% of patients developed radiographic adjacent segment pathology, but only 17% actually underwent follow-up surgery for symptomatic disease, a discrepancy echoed in other analyses.3,8 Similarly, congenital stenosis is also correlated with the development of adjacent segment degeneration and, however, has not been shown to produce higher rates of symptomatic adjacent segment disease or myelopathy.35

This study provides a basal rate of degeneration and a significantly longer observation period after fusion than is typically obtained in the postoperative setting. The observation period for the congenital fusion patients in this study is essentially equivalent to the patient's age. This corresponds to a “worst case scenario” and an upper limit of adjacent-level degeneration because a fusion performed in an older middle-aged or older person results in loss of motion at a level that may have already lost significant movement. Thus, additional loss of stiffness in these individuals may be slight.

Taken together, our findings reinforce the notion that cervical spinal fusion may contribute to the progression of adjacent-level degeneration, particularly in the midcervical spine; nevertheless, it remains to be determined to what extent this progression is clinically relevant. In one study of 87 patients who underwent ACDF, levels adjacent to the fusion were found to undergo a higher degree of postoperative degeneration, yet clinical symptoms were attributed to adjacent and nonadjacent levels at an identical rate.36 Interestingly, virtually all patients in our study—even those with advanced degeneration—were imaged for incidental indications. Although we excluded those who had undergone prior surgery, if adjacent segment degeneration had been more clinically symptomatic, certainly a higher proportion of patients would have been imaged in the setting of radiculopathy or myelopathy.

### Limitations

Limitations of this study include the uneven distribution of patients at each fused level (with predominance at C2-C3) and retrospective data collection without formal neurological evaluation. Although we excluded any patient with a diagnosis of Klippel-Feil syndrome, we cannot completely rule out the possibility of inclusion of an asymptomatic Type I Klippel-Feil syndrome patient (single congenitally fused cervical segment). However, given that Klippel-Feil syndrome entails multiple other anatomic abnormalities, typically presents before adolescence, and generally involves multiple contiguous or noncontiguous fused segments, we believe that we used the most stringent criteria possible to generate the included study cohort. In addition, although MRI would provide the ability to assess disk characteristics such as disk height and nucleus intensity, we chose to use CT imaging because of its improved spatial resolution and the existence of substantially more patient studies available for review from our database.

## CONCLUSION

Ultimately, this is the first study of patients with congenital fusion with a large enough sample to study the effects of fusion at each individual cervical level. Our findings add to the literature on adjacent segment degeneration and give credence to the notion that a fused cervical motion segment may accelerate the rate of degeneration at surrounding levels. Future investigation will need to examine the relationship, or lack thereof, between adjacent segment degeneration and onset of symptomatic adjacent segment disease.
